_about: District profiles for the Federal Reserve Districts layer. Keys match the NAME property in the GeoJSON. Drafted from public histories; each profile lists its sources.

Federal Reserve Bank of Boston.tagline: The First District: New England's Fed, a leader in payments research and community-development economics.

timeline.text: The Federal Reserve Act creates 12 districts; Boston is the natural pick for New England's textile-and-banking economy, and all 12 banks open for business on the same day in November 1914.
As New England's mills decline, the bank's economists become known for studying regional economic transition — how an old industrial economy reinvents itself.
Boston leads the Fed's work on instant payments, helping build the FedNow service launched in 2023.

Federal Reserve Bank of Boston.today: Beyond supervising New England banks, the Boston Fed runs some of the system's most visible applied research on payments technology and household finances — the plumbing of the economy that most people never see.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

Federal Reserve Bank of New York.tagline: The Second District: first among equals — home of the trading desk, the gold vault, and a permanent vote on monetary policy.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 2nd — New York State, northern New Jersey, Fairfield County (CT), Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands

quickFacts.label: Special role
quickFacts.value: Executes monetary policy; its president holds a permanent FOMC vote

timeline.text: Under Benjamin Strong, the New York Fed becomes the system's de facto leader, inventing modern open-market operations; his death in 1928 leaves a leadership vacuum many historians link to the Fed's failures in the Depression.

The fortress at 33 Liberty Street opens; its basement vault, resting on Manhattan bedrock, comes to hold the largest known concentration of monetary gold in the world — most of it belonging to foreign governments.
The bank sits at the center of the financial crisis response — Bear Stearns, AIG, and the emergency lending facilities all run through its trading desk.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York.today: Every Fed interest-rate decision is actually carried out here: the Open Market Trading Desk buys and sells securities to move the rates that ripple out to mortgages and money markets. No other regional Reserve Bank has a comparable operational role.

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.tagline: The Third District: the smallest by geography, in the city where American central banking began.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 3rd — eastern Pennsylvania, southern New Jersey, Delaware

timeline.text: Philadelphia hosts both the First and Second Banks of the United States — the country's two pre-Fed experiments with central banking, the second killed by Andrew Jackson's veto.
The city's banking pedigree earns it a Reserve Bank despite the district being the smallest in area — a nod to history as much as geography.
The bank develops a specialty in consumer credit and real-time economic indicators; its monthly manufacturing survey and 'Philly Fed index' become market-moving data.

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.today: The Philadelphia Fed is known for consumer-finance research — credit cards, mortgages, household debt — and for economic indicators that traders watch worldwide, an outsized analytical footprint for the smallest district on the map.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland.tagline: The Fourth District: the industrial heartland's Fed, with a long specialty in inflation research.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 4th — Ohio, western Pennsylvania, eastern Kentucky, northern West Virginia panhandle

timeline.text: Cleveland — then a top-six American city riding steel and oil — wins the Fourth District over rival claims from Pittsburgh and Cincinnati, which receive branches instead.
Its grand headquarters opens, vault doors among the largest ever built — monuments to an era when money meant physical gold.
As heavy industry contracts, the bank's economists become leading students of inflation measurement, developing widely used measures like median CPI.

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland.today: The Cleveland Fed's Center for Inflation Research makes it the system's reference point on the very thing most people associate with the Fed — where prices are headed — while its district tells the story of America's industrial transformation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland

Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.tagline: The Fifth District: the capital-adjacent Fed that supervises many of the nation's largest banks.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 5th — Maryland, Virginia, North and South Carolina, most of West Virginia, Washington DC

timeline.text: Richmond's selection over Baltimore is one of the 1914 committee's most contested calls — a political fight remembered in Fed lore as evidence of how hard-nosed the district-drawing really was.
Charlotte's rise as a banking capital (Bank of America, Wachovia/Wells Fargo East Coast operations) concentrates enormous supervisory responsibility in the district.
The Richmond Fed becomes a major technology and operations hub for the entire Federal Reserve System.

Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.today: With Washington's federal workforce, Charlotte's mega-banks, and the mid-Atlantic economy in its territory, the Richmond Fed pairs a heavyweight bank-supervision portfolio with research on labor markets and rural-urban economic divides.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.tagline: The Sixth District: the Southeast's Fed, a payments powerhouse for a fast-growing region.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 6th — Georgia, Alabama, Florida, and parts of Tennessee, Louisiana, Mississippi

quickFacts.label: Branches
quickFacts.value: Birmingham, Jacksonville, Miami, Nashville, New Orleans

timeline.text: Atlanta anchors the Deep South district at a time when the region's economy still ran on cotton finance.
The district's five branches — more than most — reflect the Southeast's dispersed economy, from Gulf shipping to Florida's boom-and-bust cycles.
Atlanta becomes one of the system's centers for payment processing and fintech research, mirroring the city's rise as a transaction-processing capital ('Transaction Alley').

Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.today: The Atlanta Fed processes a huge share of the nation's payments and studies the economics of the fastest-growing region in the country — including well-known tools like GDPNow, its real-time growth estimate.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.tagline: The Seventh District: the Fed of the industrial and agricultural Midwest — and of the world's derivatives markets.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 7th — northern Illinois and Indiana, southern Wisconsin, Iowa, most of Michigan

timeline.text: Chicago — the nation's second city and the hub of Midwestern finance, rail, and grain trading — is an uncontested choice for a Reserve Bank.
The district lives through the banking collapse at the Depression's epicenter of farm and factory distress.
As Chicago's futures exchanges become the world's risk-transfer capital, the bank develops deep expertise in derivatives markets and financial-market infrastructure.

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.today: The Chicago Fed watches over an economy that still makes and grows things — autos in Michigan, corn and soybeans in Iowa — while its financial-markets group monitors the exchanges where the world hedges everything from interest rates to harvests.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago

Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.tagline: The Eighth District: the monetarist Fed — and keeper of FRED, the world's favorite economic database.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 8th — Arkansas plus parts of Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi

quickFacts.label: Headquarters
quickFacts.value: One Federal Reserve Bank Plaza, St. Louis

timeline.text: St. Louis, then a top-five US city and gateway to the Mississippi Valley, anchors a district reaching into seven states — Arkansas is the only state entirely within it.

The bank becomes the intellectual home of monetarism inside the Fed, publishing money-supply data and research that challenge the system's own orthodoxy — a rare case of a regional bank as loyal opposition.
It launches FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data), which grows into the world's most widely used free economic database, alongside the FRASER digital archive of economic history.

Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.today: If you've ever seen a chart of US unemployment or GDP on the internet, odds are it came from FRED. The St. Louis Fed turned a mid-sized district into the Fed's public data window — a genuinely democratizing piece of the bureaucracy.

Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.tagline: The Ninth District: the northern frontier Fed, from the Great Lakes to Glacier — and a heavyweight in economic theory.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 9th — Minnesota, Montana, North and South Dakota, northwestern Wisconsin, Upper Michigan

timeline.text: Minneapolis — the flour-milling capital financing the wheat belt — anchors a vast, sparsely populated district stretching to the Rockies.
A partnership with the University of Minnesota makes the bank a center of the 'rational expectations' revolution in macroeconomics; several collaborators later win Nobel Prizes.
The bank becomes known for outspoken research on too-big-to-fail banks and, later, on economic opportunity gaps.

Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.today: The Minneapolis Fed pairs a frontier-sized district — much of it farm, forest, and reservation land — with some of the most ambitious pure research in the system, including its Opportunity & Inclusive Growth Institute.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.tagline: The Tenth District: the plains-and-energy Fed, host of the world's most famous economic conference — and half the reason Missouri has two Reserve Banks.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 10th — Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Wyoming, northern New Mexico, western Missouri

timeline.text: Missouri becomes the only state with two Reserve Banks — Kansas City and St. Louis. Critics then and now note that Missouri Democrats held key posts when the map was drawn; defenders point to the state's genuine role as a two-front banking gateway.
The bank's Jackson Hole Economic Symposium in Wyoming grows into the world's most watched central-banking event, where Fed chairs signal policy shifts to global markets from a mountain lodge.
The district's fortunes track wheat, cattle, and energy — the bank remains the Fed's specialist in agricultural and energy economics.

Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.today: The Kansas City Fed speaks for the rural and energy economy inside the system, and once a year — via Jackson Hole — it hosts the stage from which the world's monetary policy is previewed.

Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.tagline: The Eleventh District: the Texas Fed — oil, the border economy, and one of the fastest-growing districts in the system.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 11th — Texas, northern Louisiana, southern New Mexico

timeline.text: Dallas wins the district in the era of cotton finance — oil would soon rewrite the region's economy entirely.
The Texas oil bust and savings-and-loan collapse devastate the district's banks; the cleanup makes the Dallas Fed a hard-won expert in banking crises.
NAFTA and its successors turn the district into the Fed's listening post on US–Mexico trade and border economics.

Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.today: The Dallas Fed tracks the two forces that make its district unlike any other: the global energy market and the cross-border economy with Mexico. When oil moves, its research is where markets look for the regional read.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.tagline: The Twelfth District: the largest by far — nine states, the Pacific territories, and the world's tech economy.

quickFacts.label: District
quickFacts.value: 12th — Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Washington, plus Pacific territories

quickFacts.label: Branches
quickFacts.value: Los Angeles, Portland, Salt Lake City, Seattle

timeline.text: San Francisco anchors a district covering the entire West — then a modest slice of the US economy, today its largest regional economy by output.
The district absorbs Alaska, Hawaii, and the Pacific territories after statehood and war reshape the map, becoming the Fed's window on the Pacific Rim.

Silicon Valley's rise gives the bank a front-row seat on the technology economy; its 2023 supervision of the Silicon Valley Bank failure becomes a case study in the challenges of overseeing tech-era banking.

Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.today: Covering roughly a fifth of the US population and its most dynamic industries, the San Francisco Fed watches the economy's frontier — technology, trade with Asia, and Western housing markets — from the largest territory any Reserve Bank has ever had.
